trial_name: ARISE — Goal-Directed Resuscitation for Patients with Early Septic Shock (2014)
citation: Peake SL, Delaney A, Bailey M, et al; ARISE Investigators; ANZICS Clinical Trials Group. Goal-directed resuscitation for patients with early septic shock. N Engl J Med. 2014;371(16):1496-1506.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, randomised, parallel-group, open-label, superiority
one_liner: Protocolised 6-hour EGDT using mandatory central venous ScvO2 monitoring did not reduce 90-day all-cause mortality compared with usual care in early septic shock.

pico.population: Adults presenting to the ED with early septic shock (within 6 hours of ED presentation with fluid-refractory hypotension or lactate ≥4.0 mmol/L).
pico.intervention: Protocolised Early Goal-Directed Therapy (EGDT) for 6 hours with mandatory CVC, continuous ScvO2 monitoring, and algorithmic fluid, vasopressor, inotrope, and transfusion targets.
pico.comparison: Usual clinician-directed resuscitation and care without mandated CVP or ScvO2 targets.

background.existing_knowledge: Early Goal-Directed Therapy (EGDT) using a 6-hour protocol targeting CVP, MAP, and ScvO2 improved survival in a 2001 single-centre study by Rivers et al.
background.knowledge_gap: Over the subsequent decade, routine sepsis care evolved (earlier recognition, lactate testing, prompt antibiotics), raising doubt whether invasive protocol targets provided incremental benefit beyond contemporary usual care.
background.hypothesis: In adult emergency department patients with early septic shock, protocolised 6-hour EGDT reduces 90-day all-cause mortality compared with usual care.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, parallel-group, open-label, investigator-initiated effectiveness trial.
methods.setting: 51 emergency departments across Australia, New Zealand, Finland, Hong Kong, and Ireland; randomisation within 2 hours of meeting final eligibility criteria and within 6 hours of ED presentation.

inclusion: Age ≥18 years presenting to the ED
Refractory hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg after ≥1000 mL IV fluid challenge within 60 minutes) OR blood lactate ≥4.0 mmol/L
exclusion: Imminent death or expected survival <90 days
Inability to deliver assigned intervention within required timeframe

methods.intervention: Protocolised 6-hour EGDT with mandatory central venous catheter (CVC) and continuous ScvO2 catheter (plus arterial catheter). Hierarchical targets: SpO2 ≥93%; CVP ≥8 mmHg (unventilated) or ≥12 mmHg (ventilated) using fluid challenges; MAP 65–90 mmHg using vasopressors/vasodilators; ScvO2 ≥70% using red-cell transfusion (if haematocrit <30%) and/or dobutamine.
methods.comparison: Usual care: resuscitation and monitoring at clinician discretion without mandated targets or continuous ScvO2 monitoring.
methods.blinding: Open-label (blinding impossible for invasive procedures); objective primary endpoint minimised detection bias.
methods.sample_size_power: 1600 planned to detect a 7.6% absolute reduction in 90-day mortality (38.0% usual care to 30.4% EGDT; 20% RRR) with 90% power at alpha 0.05.
secondary_outcomes: Renal replacement therapy utilization and duration
ED, ICU, and hospital length of stay
Resuscitation volumes and blood products administered at 0–6 hours

headline_bullets: EGDT showed no benefit over usual care for 90-day all-cause mortality (18.6% vs 18.8%).
Control group mortality (18.8%) was substantially lower than historical cohorts (38% planned).
EGDT significantly increased invasive catheterization, blood transfusions, and dobutamine infusions without altering organ failure or length of stay.

outcomes_table.note: Median duration 29.4 h (IQR 15.4–52.1) vs 34.2 h (IQR 16.5–66.7); P=0.24
Shorter ED stay reflects earlier ICU transfer for protocol execution

outcomes_table.outcome: Continuous ScvO2 catheter in first 0–6 hours

safety: Any adverse event to 72 hours: 56/793 (7.1%) in EGDT vs 42/798 (5.3%) in usual care (RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.91–1.98; P=0.15)
Pneumothorax from invasive line placement: 3 patients in EGDT vs 0 in usual care
Arterial/venous bleeding or vascular puncture complications: 10 patients in EGDT vs 1 in usual care

domains.notes: Centralised randomisation with site stratification and variable block size; concealment fully preserved.
Open-label design due to invasive procedural requirements; primary endpoint (90-day mortality) is objective.

796 allocated to EGDT (4 excluded: 1 lost to follow-up, 3 declined delayed consent) and 804 allocated to usual care (8 excluded: 1 lost to follow-up, 6 declined delayed consent, 1 withdrew consent). Primary analysis was ITT on 792 vs 796 patients.
Target achievement at 6 hours was high in EGDT (SpO2 99.6%, CVP 88.9%, MAP 94.1%, ScvO2 95.3%). ScvO2 catheters used in 90.4% EGDT vs 0.4% usual care; CVC used in 89.4% EGDT vs 61.9% usual care.

Groups matched well: age 62.7 ± 16.4 vs 63.1 ± 16.5 years; APACHE II score 15.4 ± 6.5 vs 15.8 ± 6.5; lactate 6.9 ± 3.2 vs 6.7 ± 3.0 mmol/L; pre-randomisation IV fluids 2515 ± 1244 vs 2591 ± 1331 mL; median time from ED to randomisation 2.8 h vs 2.7 h.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong, supported by robust concealment, high intervention adherence, clear group separation, near-complete follow-up, and an objective primary outcome.

domains.notes: Reflects modern emergency department septic shock presentation in high-income healthcare systems with prompt baseline resuscitation.
Applicable to ED settings with well-established sepsis care pathways; less applicable to low-resource settings lacking rapid access to antimicrobials, fluids, or ICU resources.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for modern high-resource critical care systems, but extrapolation to settings without established baseline sepsis care is limited.

strengths: High protocol adherence and clear therapeutic separation between study arms
Minimal loss to follow-up for 90-day mortality primary endpoint
Prespecified statistical analysis plan published prior to study completion
limitations: Open-label design required due to device placement
Control group mortality (18.8%) was far lower than the hypothesized 38%, reducing power for small effect sizes
Minor loss of patients post-randomisation due to local delayed-consent processes

critical_appraisal.summary: ARISE is a high-quality pragmatic trial proving that invasive EGDT protocolization adds no mortality benefit over contemporary usual care in well-resourced health systems.
strengths: Rigorous central randomisation and allocation concealment
High protocol separation with minimal crossover (0.4% ScvO2 catheter in usual care)
weaknesses: Overpowered assumption for control mortality leading to lower absolute power for subtle differences

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients presenting to the emergency department with early septic shock, EGDT did not reduce all-cause mortality at 90 days compared with usual care.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: EGDT should not be routinely mandated in early septic shock resuscitation.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ED patients with early fluid-refractory septic shock or severe hyperlactatemia in resourced systems.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Early fluids, rapid antibiotics, vasopressors, or clinical monitoring are unnecessary.
implementation_caveats: Ensure prompt administration of antimicrobials and initial IV fluid resuscitation before considering invasive lines
Reserve central venous catheterization and ScvO2 monitoring for specific clinical indications rather than standard protocolized bundles

controversies.notes: Post-publication correspondence noted that substantial pre-randomisation fluids (~2.5 L) and prompt usual care lowered mortality (~19% vs historical ~38%), reducing the window for additional intervention benefit.
Specific static physiological targets (CVP 8–12, ScvO2 ≥70%) were shown to lack specific clinical value over routine clinician-directed care.

context_related_trials.relation: Original single-centre trial that established EGDT; ARISE demonstrated that its findings did not translate to modern care systems.
US trial conducted concurrently with ARISE showing no benefit of protocolised EGDT over usual care.
UK trial conducted concurrently with ARISE showing no mortality benefit and higher costs with EGDT.
Individual patient data meta-analysis of ARISE, ProCESS, and ProMISe confirming no survival benefit for EGDT across all subgroups.

unresolved_questions: Whether specific unstudied subgroups in resource-limited settings benefit from central line protocolization
Role of advanced non-invasive hemodynamic monitoring techniques in early septic shock

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Protocolised EGDT increases invasive monitoring, fluids, transfusions, and inotropes without improving 90-day survival compared to modern standard care.
